newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asian Gold - Losses extended on long liquidation.
newsitem.headline: Asian Gold - Losses extended on long liquidation.

text.p: A fresh rash of sales overnight sparked heavy long liquidation in Asian gold trading on Friday, pushing the precious metal to new three-year lows, with no respite from the pounding seen in the near term, dealers said. "Most of the sales we have seen have been long liquidations by traders who had been figuring we'd seen the worst," said Jonathan Spall, head of precious metals for Deutsche Bank AG in Hong Kong.

Spot gold's rally to a high of US$357.40 an ounce on Tuesday convinced many dealers that prices had every chance of nudging further up to $360, but the overnight sales in the U.S. on Thursday proved them wrong, Spall said.
Hong Kong spot gold was quoted at $344.75/345.05 an ounce at 0500 GMT on Friday, after hitting its lowest levels since September 1993, and was also down from the market's opening at $345.50/346.00.
Rumours of central bank gold sales continued to haunt Asian markets.

"The sharp losses in spot gold was partly attributable to talks that central banks were selling gold in the New York market on Thursday, although this has not been confirmed, yet," said Keiji Yanagida, a dealer at Mitsubishi Corp in Tokyo.

Hong Kong's Spall concurred, noting that central bank sale rumours did not help the market, while a senior Singapore dealer said European banks were selling gold, but he still felt the market was oversold.
Dealers in Asia saw very little cheer on the horizon.
"We don't see the bottom yet. The next target would be $340 an ounce, and after breaching that level, a tumble to $320 cannot be ruled out," Mitsubishi Yanagida said.
"Obviously we've now made fresh lows, it's got every chance of going lower again," Deutsche's Spall said.
Central bank sale anxiety was compounded in Asia by a strong U.S. dollar and a muscular U.S. stock market. Both are taken as bearish indicators for the gold price trend.

Widespread expectations that the U.S. government will not hike its interest rates at next week's FOMC (Federal Open Market Committee) meeting may also be bearish for the spot gold market, Tokyo dealers said.
The bearish cloud extended to Singapore, but a senior trader said he would rather remain long in case of a price rebound.
"The fund managers are depressing the market and prices are low, I do not want to be caught short in such a market, I would rather be long as prices may bounce up" he said.
In the options markets, gold volatilities were soaring through the roof, traders said.
"We're paying at the moment around the 12.5 percent mark in the one month term," said one options trader, noting that in mid-January one month volatility was 10.5 percent.

"Now that volatilities are going up higher in the shorter term, (players) are stopping out and have to go and buy it back, or they're going to be losing too much money with the movement of the spot," he added.
Even physical demand in Asia, said to be trotting at a healthy clip on Chinese New Year and Moslem festivity demand, failed to provide much of a golden lining.

Singapore gold premiums were firm, but unchanged from last week at between 100 and 120 U.S. cents an ounce over London cash prices and sources saw gold prices plunging further once Asian demand dried up after the holiday season.

Hong Kong premiums also remained unchanged from last week at around 150 U.S. cents over the spot market, but kilobar availability had improved as suppliers looked to liquidate ahead of closing for Chinese New Year from February 6 to February 9.
